subject: [Skylet] Reap descendants when parent dies (subreaper) or wedges alive (zombie sweep) (#9672)
message:
[Skylet] Reap descendants when parent dies (subreaper) or wedges alive (zombie sweep) (#9672)

* [Skylet] Reap orphaned descendants via subreaper + PPID-transition watch

When a sky job's `run:` block backgrounds a multi-process workload (e.g.
`python server.py & ; sleep 86400` or any pattern where the wrapper bash
outlives the workload's parent process), and the parent then dies
abnormally (SIGKILL, OOM, segfault, user `pkill`), the workload's
children reparent to PID 1 (the pod's bootstrap bash on k8s) and keep
holding whatever resource they had: GPU contexts, RAM, listening
sockets, open files, IPC objects.

The existing `subprocess_daemon` doesn't clean them up: its watch loop
is gated on the wrapper bash being alive, and `process.children(recursive=True)`
no longer finds the orphans once they've left the wrapper's tree.

This change closes both gaps:

- `sky/utils/subprocess_utils.set_child_subreaper`: tiny helper that
  calls `prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, 1)` on the calling process.
  Linux-only; silent no-op elsewhere and on pre-3.4 kernels.

- `sky/skylet/log_lib.run_with_log`: wires the helper in as `preexec_fn`
  for the workload `subprocess.Popen`. Since the subreaper attribute is
  preserved across execve, the launched shell becomes a subreaper for
  its descendants — orphans reparent to the shell instead of to PID 1
  and stay inside the tree the daemon walks. Caller-supplied
  `preexec_fn` is chained, not replaced.

- `sky/skylet/subprocess_daemon`: inside the existing watch loop, also
  track each descendant's PPID across ticks. When a descendant's PPID
  transitions to the watched process's PID (the kernel's signal that
  it was just adopted by the subreaper), SIGTERM it immediately. The
  existing final-sweep behavior on parent/proc exit is unchanged.

The fix is resource-agnostic — it solves the GPU-VRAM-leak symptom that
prompted the investigation, but the same code path also catches RAM
leaks, port leaks, FD leaks, IPC leaks from the same root cause. The
new smoke test exercises it with CPU-only `multiprocessing.spawn`
workers; GPU is not required to reproduce or to verify the fix.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Skylet] Also reap workers under SIGTERM-wedged parents

The PPID-transition watch added earlier catches the case where the
workload's parent process dies abnormally (SIGKILL, OOM, segfault, user
pkill) — the workers reparent to the subreaper and the daemon SIGTERMs
them on the next tick.

It does not catch the case where the parent receives a graceful SIGTERM,
installs a handler that raises an exception out of an unsafe spot
(e.g. mid-syscall during init), and ends up wedged alive. The children
the parent was supposed to wait() on become zombies under the wedged
parent, and any still-alive sibling workers stay parked under it forever
holding their resources. There is no PPID transition, so the existing
watch never fires.

This change adds a wedge sweep in the same watch loop:

- subprocess_daemon._zombie_wedge_sweep: age each zombie descendant
  across ticks. When one has been zombie for longer than
  SKYPILOT_ZOMBIE_GRACE_SECONDS (default 30 s), the parent isn't just
  slow, it's stuck — SIGKILL it. The still-alive sibling workers then
  reparent to the subreaper and the existing PPID-transition machinery
  cleans them up on the next tick. Excluded SIGKILL targets: PID 1,
  the watched subreaper, and the outer SkyPilot orchestrator parent.

- SKYPILOT_REAP_WEDGED_PARENTS env var (default '1') as an opt-out
  switch, in case the new behavior surprises a specific workload that
  legitimately leaves long-lived zombies.

- tests/test_yamls/orphan_reap_sigkill.yaml + orphan_reap_sigterm_wedge.yaml:
  new YAML fixtures, matching the tests/test_yamls/ pattern other
  smoke tests use. Refactors the existing SIGKILL test to load its
  config from the fixture (was an inline heredoc); adds a new SIGTERM-
  wedge smoke test that exercises the new sweep end-to-end on
  Kubernetes.

Verified locally by exercising the real log_lib.run_with_log +
subprocess_utils.kill_process_daemon code paths against a Python
process that installs a self-wedging SIGTERM handler and forks both
a long-lived worker and a short-lived helper. Without the fix the
wedged parent and worker survive indefinitely; with the fix both are
gone within ~33 s of the SIGTERM (30 s zombie grace + a few ticks of
SIGKILL escalation and PPID-transition cleanup). The PR #9672 SIGKILL
path remains: workers cleaned in ~2 s.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Skylet] Address PR #9672 review feedback

Four concrete fixes based on review comments + empirical verification:

1. Route daemon output to a log file. kill_process_daemon spawns the
   daemon with stdout=stderr=DEVNULL, so prior `print(file=sys.stderr)`
   calls in the wedge sweep were dropped. New `_log()` helper appends
   to ~/.sky/subprocess_daemon-<proc_pid>.log so wedge-kill events
   leave an audit trail.

2. Escalate SIGTERM → SIGKILL instead of immediate SIGKILL on the
   wedged ancestor. Empirically (test on the canonical vLLM-style
   signal.pause() wedge): a single SIGTERM unwinds the wedge cleanly
   in ~1 s. The 5 s grace before SIGKILL lets such processes complete
   atexit hooks and child cleanup; truly-unkillable wedges still get
   force-killed after the grace. New `_term_then_kill()` helper.

3. Correct the `run_with_log` preexec_fn safety comment. The prior
   claim ("not multi-threaded at this point") was wrong — empirical
   instrumentation showed `run_with_log` is reached from
   ThreadPoolExecutor workers in the API server path. The code is
   nonetheless safe because (a) the libc handle is resolved at module

The Problem-2 zombie-wedge sweep assumed "a healthy program never leaves a
child zombie for >grace seconds". That is false for SkyPilot's own
long-lived, event-driven daemons — the jobs/serve/pool controller and its
executors legitimately carry a transient child zombie past the 60s grace
while actively reaping other children. The sweep then SIGKILLed them and
cascaded up the controller tree, producing CONTROLLER_FAILED in

test_pool_job_cancel_recovery (all green on master).

   and never reaped it. The watchdog double-forks (daemonize()); the
   first-fork parent exits within ~hundreds of ms but lingered as a zombie
   under the caller until CPython GC'd the dangling Popen. On a busy host
   (the controller calls run_with_log -> kill_process_daemon constantly)
   these self-inflicted zombies accumulated — and were exactly what the
   wedge sweep misread. Reap the intermediate in a background thread so the
   hot path is never blocked.

   daemon now tracks, per parent pid, the last time it was observed to reap

   has a zombie older than the grace period AND has not reaped any child
   within the grace window. This preserves Problem 2 (a signal.pause()
   wedge reaps nothing -> still killed) while sparing healthy daemons.

subject: Fix Ray helper crash on externally-managed Python (PEP 668) (#9896)
message:
Fix Ray helper crash on externally-managed Python (PEP 668) (#9896)

* [Core] Set UV_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES in Ray helper --system fallback

The Ray helper (~/sky_templates/ray/start_cluster) ensures ray[default] is
present via `uv pip install ... || uv pip install --system ...`. On a
bring-your-own image with no virtualenv and an externally-managed system
Python (PEP 668, e.g. Ubuntu 24.04+), the first attempt fails (no venv) and
the --system fallback also fails because uv refuses to modify an
externally-managed Python. This crashed multi-node cluster startup (head
exits code 2, workers SIGKILLed) even when the correct Ray version was
already installed in the image.

Set UV_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=true on the --system fallback so the install
succeeds on externally-managed Python. When the required Ray is already
present, Ray stays at the image version.

message:
[Buildkite] Only fail on 0 pipeline steps when every generated file is empty (#9911)

[Buildkite] Only fail on 0 steps when every pipeline file is empty

generate_pipeline.py always writes more than one pipeline file (release and
quick-tests-core). The 0-steps guard added in #9903 fired per file, so a
targeted `pytest -k`/file-pattern run that matches tests in only one of the
files made the other file empty and failed the whole pipeline-upload step —
even though a valid, non-empty pipeline was produced for the matched group.

Move the guard up a level: skip writing an empty file (Buildkite rejects
empty step groups anyway) and fail loudly only when *every* generated file
is empty, i.e. collection matched nothing anywhere. That still catches the
genuine misconfiguration #9903 targeted (unrecognised args / wrong cloud
filter / missing env file collecting 0 tests everywhere) without breaking
legitimate single-group filters.

_dump_pipeline_to_file now returns the step count it wrote; main() sums the
counts across files and only exits non-zero when the total is 0.

subject: [Jobs] Don't leak request env vars into spawned consolidation controllers (#9665)
message:
[Jobs] Don't leak request env vars into spawned consolidation controllers (#9665)

* [Jobs] Don't leak request env vars into spawned consolidation controllers

In consolidation mode, when an in-flight request handler spawns the local
controller subprocess chain (worker -> bash -> scheduler -> nohup ->
sky.jobs.controller), the controller inherits the worker's os.environ.
That env has just been polluted mid-request by
override_request_env_and_config's os.environ.update(request_body.env_vars).
Anything the client had with a SKYPILOT_ prefix (notably
SKYPILOT_API_SERVER_ENDPOINT) ends up baked into the long-lived controller
for the rest of its life. When recovery later calls sdk.api_start(),
get_server_url() returns the leaked endpoint, is_api_server_local()
returns False, and managed jobs fail with "Unable to start local API
server: server endpoint is set to ...".

Fix in two layers:

1. Plumbing fix: capture a clean snapshot of os.environ at API server
   startup (and once per worker process at spawn time, after plugin init),
   then plumb an explicit env= kwarg through _consolidated_launch ->
   backend.run_on_head -> CommandRunner.run_driver ->
   LocalProcessCommandRunner.run -> log_lib.run_with_log ->
   subprocess.Popen. The first subprocess in the chain (bash) now starts
   with a clean env; every descendant inherits clean env. controller_envs
   are layered back on top via the explicit `export` lines already
   prepended to the run script.

2. Belt-and-suspenders: recovery_strategy.py's ENV_VARS_TO_CLEAR (already
   cleared before sdk.api_start()) now includes SKY_API_SERVER_URL_ENV_VAR.
   This lets controllers spawned with a polluted env (during a rolling
   upgrade, or before this fix lands) self-heal at api_start time.
   get_server_url and is_api_server_local are functools.lru_cache'd, so
   the cache is also invalidated before api_start to ensure the cleared
   env actually takes effect even if the cache was populated earlier in
   the process's life.

Serve consolidation (sky/serve/server/impl.py::up) mirrors the same
plumbing — its backend.run_on_head(...) for the serve controller also
takes the clean-env kwarg.

test_check_server_healthy_or_start_rechecks_status mocks

Inside the real check_server_healthy(), the auto-generated

Concretely, this surfaces as

at sky/client/sdk.py:2927 (remote_api_version >= 30) when

* Address review: fix env leak in LocalProcessCommandRunner directly

Per @hf3cc3e4fc8f43668's review: LocalProcessCommandRunner is the only CommandRunner

subprocess.Popen. SSH/Slurm runners apply env via remote shell exports,

[metrics] Make GPU/endpoint metrics federation observable + readable timeouts (#9915)

* [metrics] Make GPU/endpoint metrics federation observable + readable timeouts

The /gpu-metrics and /endpoints-metrics endpoints federate each remote
Kubernetes context's Prometheus via a kubectl port-forward + /federate scrape.
When a context timed out, the only signal was:

    Failed to get metrics for context <ctx>:

an empty string, because the per-context asyncio.wait_for raises
asyncio.TimeoutError whose str() is ''. There was also no visibility into where

subject: [Kubernetes] Fix pod recovery deadlock against Kueue's managed finalizer (#9918)
message:
[Kubernetes] Fix pod recovery deadlock against Kueue's managed finalizer (#9918)

When recreating a pod with the same name as one that is still terminating
(e.g. after a node/pod failure), provisioning fails with 409 "object is
being deleted: pods ... already exists" and recovery aborts with
StopFailoverError. Two things keep the old object around:

1. Kueue keeps its kueue.x-k8s.io/managed finalizer on a terminating
   pod-group pod until it observes a replacement; the finalizer blocks
   garbage-collection. The replacement (same name) cannot be created while
   the old object exists -> deadlock.
2. Even with no finalizer, the object survives its
   terminationGracePeriodSeconds (for Ray pods this is the preemption-hook
   timeout, which can be minutes), so the same-named create keeps 409-ing.

Route the existing 409 "object is being deleted" handler through a single
_force_remove_terminating_pod() that, in order: strips the Kueue finalizer
(via a JSON patch -- a strategic-merge patch is a no-op on the finalizers
list), force-deletes with grace period 0, waits until the object is gone,
then recreates. Kueue then admits the new pod as the replacement and does
not re-add the finalizer. The finalizer is stripped before the force-delete
because a force-delete cannot clear a finalizer-held pod. Non-Kueue clusters
are unaffected: there is no finalizer to strip, and the force-delete clears
the stale terminating pod as before.

Also delete pods with --wait=false in the kubernetes recovery smoke test;
kubectl delete otherwise blocks on finalizer removal (which only happens
after recovery recreates the pod), so the test would hang before reaching
the recovery step.

Tested:
- Added unit tests (TestCreatePodFinalizerHandling) covering the Kueue
  finalizer path and the non-Kueue stale-pod path.
- pytest tests/unit_tests/kubernetes/test_provision.py passes.
- Ran tests/smoke_tests/test_cluster_job.py::test_kubernetes_recovery
  end-to-end against a Kueue-enabled Kubernetes cluster: passes (recovery
  recreates the deleted head/worker pods after force-removing the
  terminating ones).

subject: Executor should not skip WAITING requests (#9928)
message:
Executor should not skip WAITING requests (#9928)

* [Server] Execute dequeued WAITING requests, not just PENDING

A request parked in WAITING (waiting to resume from a retry backoff or an
external continue-condition) is re-enqueued onto the task queue once it is
ready to run again. But _request_execution_wrapper only proceeded when the
dequeued request was PENDING and silently skipped everything else, so a
re-enqueued WAITING request was dropped on the floor: its queue entry was
consumed, no worker ran it, and it was stranded in WAITING forever with
nothing left to reschedule it.

Add RequestStatus.executable_statuses() = {PENDING, WAITING} and gate the
wrapper on it, so a dequeued WAITING request transitions to RUNNING and
executes like PENDING. Other statuses (RUNNING, finished, CANCELLED) are
still skipped. Also raise the skip log from debug to warning so an
unexpected skip is visible instead of silent.

Tested: added test_waiting_request_is_executed_not_skipped asserting a
dequeued WAITING request runs to SUCCEEDED.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Test] Smoke test: retry-until-up WAITING request is re-executed

End-to-end regression for the previous commit. A --retry-until-up launch that
exhausts launchable resources parks its request in WAITING and re-enqueues it;
the worker must re-execute it. Pre-fix the re-enqueued WAITING request was
skipped and stranded, so the cluster never progressed.

Kubernetes-only and size-independent: requests 100 x 1-CPU nodes. Per-node
1 CPU fits any node's capacity (passes feasibility), but 100 nodes fit no
single smoke node, so the pods sit Pending and provisioning fails into the
retry/WAITING path. Pending pods consume no allocatable, so the test does not
disturb others sharing the cluster. Asserts the request reaches WAITING and
then RUNNING again (the re-execution); pre-fix the second wait times out.

subject: [Jobs] Run managed-job-status-refresh as a main-process thread (#9731)
message:
[Jobs] Run managed-job-status-refresh as a main-process thread (#9731)

* [Jobs] Run managed-job-status-refresh as a main-process thread

The managed-job-status-refresh daemon was scheduled on the shared
executor task queue, which in HA mode lets the daemon drift to a
different replica from the controllers it spawned: a BrokenProcessPool
or worker SIGKILL on the holder pops the daemon onto a sibling replica,
where ha_recovery_for_consolidation_mode runs controller_process_alive
against PIDs that live in another pod's PID namespace, declares them
all dead, and respawns a parallel set of controllers.

Bind the daemon's lifecycle to the API server main process by running
it as a thread (started in the supervisor, not in lifespan — lifespan
runs per uvicorn worker).  The daemon, the consolidation_mode lock it
holds, and the controllers it spawns now share a single process / pod
lifecycle.

The PG advisory lock can still go silently stale while main is alive
(idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, NLB idle, RDS restart, etc.); add
PostgresLock.is_session_alive() so the thread probes the lock's
underlying session every 5s and SIGTERMs itself on loss, letting K8s
restart the pod and the remaining replicas re-elect a leader.

Tests:
- PostgresLock.is_session_alive: not-acquired / no-connection /
  SELECT 1 success / SELECT 1 raises.
- ManagedJobRefreshDaemonThread state machine: dispatches PostgresLock
  vs other DistributedLock for liveness, sends SIGTERM to self on
  lock loss, gates start on consolidation mode.

* Refine

Signed-off-by: ubda012a9867b6dfc <ubda012a9867b6dfc@users.invalid>

* Address gemini-code-assist review

- Touch the rolling-restart signal file only after we hold the lock.
  With the daemon thread starting on every replica, standby replicas
  blocked in acquire() would otherwise leave a stale signal file
  forever and update_managed_jobs_statuses would early-return on them.
- Decouple the lock probe from the event-loop sleep. The inner loop
  used to sleep events.EVENT_CHECKING_INTERVAL_SECONDS (20 s) per
  iteration, so the lock probe fired ~20 s apart instead of the
  intended 5 s. Now the loop ticks at 1 s with separate cadences for
  the probe and the event run.
- In the outer except block, distinguish between "acquire() itself
  failed" (retry) and "we held the lock and the session died"
  (SIGTERM). Otherwise a transient recovery failure plus a lost PG
  session would keep us in the retry loop as a stale leader while
  another replica acquired the lock cleanly.

Tests cover the three new branches.

* Fix pylint and test_daemons after refactor

- Move sky.jobs.constants to top-level imports
- Drop redundant except (SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt) re-raise
- Remove TestConsolidationEventInstancePersistence cases that referenced
  the now-deleted _managed_job_consolidation_mode_lock and managed_job
  event in sky.server.daemons (logic moved to ManagedJobRefreshDaemonThread)

* [Jobs] Restore managed_job_status_refresh_event stubs for pickle compat

After the managed-job-status-refresh daemon was rewritten as an in-process
thread, the pickled InternalRequestDaemon rows from older server versions
in HA deployments reference daemons.managed_job_status_refresh_event and
daemons.should_skip_managed_job_status_refresh via their event_fn /
should_skip attributes. pickle.loads raises AttributeError on every poll
of those rows, generating a flood of internal /api/get 500 responses
during a rolling upgrade.

Restore both symbols as no-op stubs so that pickle.loads succeeds. The
daemon-orphan cleanup path will then delete those orphan rows because no
matching INTERNAL_REQUEST_DAEMONS entry exists for the pickled daemon id.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Jobs] Kill local job controllers on consolidation lock loss

When the managed-job refresh daemon's PostgreSQL session dies
(idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, NLB idle, pg_terminate_backend,
etc.), the advisory lock is released server-side and another replica
can immediately acquire it. Until now, _suicide_on_lock_loss just
sent SIGTERM to the API server and relied on the up-to-60s drain to
eventually free the controllers via kernel PID-namespace cleanup.
During that window, the new leader's ha_recovery sees ALIVE jobs
with no local controller and spawns fresh ones — splitting writes
with the still-running old controllers.

Tighten the window from "until drain finishes" to ~0:

* Add scheduler.kill_local_job_controllers() that reads the local
  controller PID file, skips dead/stale records via
  controller_process_alive(), and SIGTERMs each live PID. Idempotent
  and best-effort.

* In _suicide_on_lock_loss, re-touch the recovery signal file (so any
  in-flight submit_jobs short-circuits maybe_start_controllers) and
  call kill_local_job_controllers() before sending the API-server
  SIGTERM. Both new steps are best-effort and never block the SIGTERM.

The graceful-shutdown path in uvicorn does NOT need this — while the
session stays alive, the daemon thread holds the lock until the
supervisor exits, and at that instant the kernel SIGKILLs every
process in the pod's PID namespace, so the controllers cannot
outlive the leader transition.

Tests: unit tests for kill_local_job_controllers (live/stale/missing
file/permission errors); _suicide_on_lock_loss touches the file and
kills before SIGTERM, in that order; touch failure does not block
SIGTERM.

* Use pathlib.Path.unlink(missing_ok=True)

Replace the try/except FileNotFoundError around signal_file.unlink()
with the missing_ok=True kwarg, which has been available since
Python 3.8 and is the idiomatic form used elsewhere in the codebase.

* Update sky/jobs/managed_job_refresh_thread.py

Co-authored-by: gemini-code-assist[bot] <176961590+gemini-code-assist[bot]@users.noreply.github.com>

* [Jobs] Stop refresh thread after _suicide_on_lock_loss

`_become_leader_and_run` returns normally only after the inner loop's
probe detected lock loss and called `_suicide_on_lock_loss` — every
other exit path raises. The outer `run()` loop was catching that
return and immediately re-entering, where:

  - `is_locked()` returns True (stale local `_acquired` flag; only
    `is_session_alive()` knows the server-side lock is gone),
  - the acquire branch is skipped,
  - `ha_recovery_for_consolidation_mode()` runs,
  - and `scheduler.maybe_start_controllers()` is called without
    `from_scheduler=True`, so the recovery signal-file gate at
    scheduler.py:237 is bypassed.

Fresh controllers get spawned via `launch_new_process_tree` (nohup +
setsid) under a now-released lock. Meanwhile, the new leader on the
other replica is doing the same — both replicas run controllers for
the same managed jobs for the duration of the API server drain
(~60s), splitting writes to managed-job state. This is exactly the
failure mode `_suicide_on_lock_loss` was supposed to prevent. The
preceding "Kill local job controllers on consolidation lock loss"
commit made it strictly worse: now the suicide kills all controllers,
so the re-entry sees `alive=0` and faithfully spawns a fresh set
rather than no-op'ing on `alive == wanted`.

Add a `return` after the normal-return path so the thread stops
instead of looping. New test covers the invariant: `run()` calls
`_become_leader_and_run` exactly once when it returns normally.

* [Jobs] Touch recovery signal file before acquiring consolidation lock

Restore the pre-refactor ordering: the recovery signal file must exist
before we block on acquire(), so that during a rolling update no new
controller can be started on this replica before recovery runs. Add a
regression test pinning the touch-before-acquire contract.

subject: [API] Fix BrokenProcessPool when cancel hits an idle worker (#9742)
message:
[API] Fix BrokenProcessPool when cancel hits an idle worker (#9742)

* [API] Fix BrokenProcessPool when cancel hits an idle worker

A cancel reads request.pid and sends SIGTERM. Because worker PIDs are
long-lived across many requests, a stale RUNNING row can route SIGTERM
to a worker that has already finished that request and is now idle in
concurrent.futures._process_worker's call_queue.get(block=True). The
bare _sigterm_handler raises KeyboardInterrupt unconditionally — it's
unhandled there, the worker dies, the pool is marked BROKEN, and every
in-flight future plus subsequent submits fail with BrokenProcessPool.

Two layers:

1. set_return_value falls back to pickle_and_encode when a plugin
   encoder raises, so an encoder bug can no longer leave a row stuck
   in RUNNING (which is what populates stale pids for cancel to find
   later).

2. Worker subprocesses install _gated_sigterm_handler instead of the
   eager one. It only raises KeyboardInterrupt while
   _request_execution_wrapper is inside its protected try-block; when
   the worker is idle, the SIGTERM is latched into _pending_sigterm
   and honored at the next wrapper entry — preserving cancel semantics
   without killing the worker.

Worker.run keeps the eager handler so shutdown signals (kubelet,
ctrl-c) still abort the scheduler cleanly.

* [API] Address PR review feedback

- Move `_in_request_execution = True` inside the `try` block. A SIGTERM
  landing between the assignment and the `try:` statement would raise
  KeyboardInterrupt with no `finally` on the stack to clear the flag —
  the worker would carry _in_request_execution=True forever and the
  next idle SIGTERM would raise from call_queue.get() and break the
  pool, defeating the gate entirely.
- Use `os.write` instead of `logger.info` inside the signal handler.
  Python's logging module is not async-signal-safe; if the main thread
  is holding the logging lock when SIGTERM arrives, calling
  `logger.info` from the handler deadlocks. Move the human-readable
  logger.info to wrapper entry where the latch is consumed.
- Drop the return value to `None` on encoder failure instead of
  falling back to `pickle_and_encode`. All request-specific serializers
  explicitly guard `if return_value is not None`, so None persists
  cleanly as JSON `null`. The previous pickle-fallback produced a
  base64 string that custom serializers (e.g. `serialize_status`,
  which iterates the value as a list of clusters) would crash on,
  re-raising during the row commit and leaving the row stuck in
  RUNNING — the very state we're trying to avoid.
- Add a unit test for the encoder-failure path that asserts
  set_return_value swallows the exception and stores None.

* [API] Drop honor-on-entry; SIGTERM-to-idle just swallowed

Honoring a latched SIGTERM at the next wrapper entry caused real
collateral: a SIGTERM landing on an executor worker just after the
previous request's `finally` cleared `_in_request_execution` would
flag `_pending_sigterm`, and the next unrelated request dispatched
to that worker raised KeyboardInterrupt immediately. On managed-jobs
controllers this manifested as repeated PENDING -> STARTING retries
(~5x slower scheduling vs master on
test_managed_jobs_cancellation_aws).

The latch isn't needed: cancellation already targets a specific pid,
so a SIGTERM that arrives after the request finishes is genuinely
stale and safe to drop. Swallow it in the handler; pool stays intact.

subject: [Serve] Fix consolidation-mode detection in wait_service_registration codegen subprocess (#9942)
message:
[Serve] Fix consolidation-mode detection in wait_service_registration codegen subprocess (#9942)

* [Serve] Fix consolidation-mode detection in wait_service_registration codegen

The codegen subprocess spawned by ServeCodeGen.wait_service_registration
inherits SKYPILOT_GLOBAL_CONFIG pointing to the client override config, which
lacks serve.controller.consolidation_mode=true. The subprocess reads the server
config from the client override path and incorrectly concludes it is NOT in
consolidation mode. This causes it to wait for a job_lib job status that never
comes (the controller is a local subprocess, not a managed job), timing out
after the 300-second CONTROLLER_SETUP_TIMEOUT with "Failed to start the
controller process within 300 seconds."

Fix by baking IS_SKYPILOT_JOB_CONTROLLER=true into the generated shell command
when the API server is in consolidation mode, so the subprocess detects the
correct mode regardless of the SKYPILOT_GLOBAL_CONFIG value.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* simplify f-string per review

* [Jobs] Fix IS_SKYPILOT_JOB_CONTROLLER env leak from start_controller()

start_controller() mutated os.environ[IS_SKYPILOT_JOB_CONTROLLER] before
spawning the controller subprocess. This was harmless before PR #9731 because
the daemon ran in a child process with its own isolated os.environ (cleaned up
by the executor's finally block). After #9731 the daemon runs as a main-process
thread, so the mutation leaks permanently into the API server's os.environ.

The leak causes serve_utils.is_consolidation_mode(pool=False) to return True
for all serve requests on any --deploy server, silently pushing sky serve up
into consolidation mode even when serve.controller.consolidation_mode is not
configured. This then triggers the codegen-subprocess timeout fixed in the
companion change to serve_utils.py.

Fix: bake the env var into the shell command (export IS_SKYPILOT_JOB_CONTROLLER=true;
...) instead of mutating os.environ, so only the controller subprocess gets it.

subject: [Server] Tolerate unresolvable request entrypoint in Request.decode (#9946)
message:
[Server] Tolerate unresolvable request entrypoint in Request.decode (#9946)

* [Server] Tolerate unresolvable request entrypoint in Request.decode

The request `entrypoint` is pickled by reference (module + qualname) in
`Request.encode()` and unpickled by the client in `Request.decode()` -- but
the client never actually invokes it. When the client is older than the
server, the server may reference a symbol the client lacks (e.g. a
newly-added `sky.core` function), and the by-reference unpickle raises
`AttributeError`/`ImportError`, failing the entire request. This is what
made `sky.down` crash against newer servers after #9916.

Decode the entrypoint through a helper that falls back to a placeholder when
the reference can't be resolved, since the value is never called on the
client. This hardens against any future server-only entrypoint symbol
reintroducing this class of version-skew breakage.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Server] Tighten type annotations on entrypoint decode helpers

Address review: annotate `_decode_entrypoint` as `Optional[Callable]` (the
encoded entrypoint may be the empty pickled value, which decodes to None),
and annotate `_unresolved_entrypoint` args; its return is `NoReturn` since it
always raises.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [Server] Keep _decode_entrypoint return as Callable to satisfy mypy

`Optional[Callable]` is incompatible with the `Request.entrypoint` field
(typed `Callable`) and would propagate into the executor call sites
(`request.entrypoint(...)`). The decode path always yields a callable for
real requests and falls back to the `_unresolved_entrypoint` callable on
failure, so a non-Optional return is accurate and keeps the change scoped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

message:
[Test] Key exclusive concurrency group on --env-file, not build id (#9949)

Exclusive smoke steps (--exclusive) are serialized via a Buildkite
concurrency group. Keying it on BUILDKITE_BUILD_ID only serializes steps
within one build, so two exclusive builds targeting the same server (a
re-triggered run, or a deploy-and-test command racing a manual run) can run
server-mutating tests concurrently and corrupt each other.

Key the group on a hash of the --env-file value instead, so all exclusive
runs against the same target serialize regardless of which build triggered
them. Fall back to the build id when no --env-file is given (each build
isolated, as before).

[Test] Fix flaky multi-context Kubernetes cloud-cmd smoke tests (#9957)

[Test] Pin cloud-cmd helper cluster to the target cluster's context

The Kubernetes cloud-cmd smoke tests launch a helper "cloud-cmd" cluster to
run kubectl, then assert on the resources of a separately launched target
cluster. On an API server with multiple Kubernetes contexts, the target and
helper clusters can land on different contexts. The helper is a regular
(non-controller) cluster, so its kubectl uses the pod's own in-cluster
credentials and only reaches its own cluster (the multi-context kubeconfig is
uploaded only to controller clusters) -- making the assertions flaky depending
on placement.

Launch the target cluster first, resolve the context it landed on, and pin the
helper cluster to the same context so kubectl observes the target cluster's
resources.

subject: [Core] Mark non-security MD5/SHA1 hashes with usedforsecurity=False (#9972)
message:
[Core] Mark non-security MD5/SHA1 hashes with usedforsecurity=False (#9972)

* [Core] Mark non-security MD5/SHA1 hashes with usedforsecurity=False

These hashlib.md5/sha1 calls derive identifiers, cache keys, and resource
names from non-secret inputs (usernames, paths, region/subscription ids,
cluster/host names, wheel/catalog contents). None protects a secret or
makes an authentication decision -- passwords use bcrypt via crypt_ctx and
auth is enforced by oauth2-proxy / SSO. Pass usedforsecurity=False so
weak-hash scanners (CWE-328) stop flagging them. The flag does not change
any digest value, so all derived ids, cache keys and names are unchanged.

* [Core] Address review: avoid split hexdigest() call in oauth2_proxy

Compute the digest first, then slice, instead of splitting the empty
hexdigest() parentheses across lines. yapf-stable and more readable.

subject: [Jobs] Wait after acquiring the consolidation lock before recovery (#9954)
message:
[Jobs] Wait after acquiring the consolidation lock before recovery (#9954)

* [Jobs] Wait after acquiring the consolidation lock before recovery

During a rolling restart of a consolidation-mode API server, the new
leader can acquire the consolidation lock the moment the old main process
exits, but that pod's detached job controllers are not killed until the
container is torn down a moment later. Running ha_recovery in that window
resets jobs that the dying old controllers briefly re-claim, stamping
soon-dead PIDs back onto them; update_managed_jobs_statuses then marks the
otherwise-healthy jobs FAILED_CONTROLLER (a split brain across the upgrade
overlap).

Wait briefly after acquiring the lock before running recovery so the prior
container and its controllers are fully gone first. The recovery signal
file stays in place during the wait, so controller starts and the
FAILED_CONTROLLER sweep remain gated and in-flight controllers are
untouched. After the wait, re-verify the lock is still held before
recovering (the wait widens the window for a silently-stale PostgresLock
session); otherwise step down via the existing lock-loss path rather than
run a second recovery loop.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Fh7ZZwmvfVeV3fHzjV2ACi

  acquiring the lock (the constant is always positive).

  finally unlinks the signal file, but the lock-loss step-down re-touches

subject: [Jobs] Don't re-issue STARTING for resumed JobGroup tasks on controller restart (#9939)
message:
[Jobs] Don't re-issue STARTING for resumed JobGroup tasks on controller restart (#9939)

When the jobs controller restarts while a JobGroup has in-flight tasks,
`_run_job_group` resumes every non-terminal task. The prepare loop called
`set_starting` for all of them, but `set_starting` only transitions
PENDING->STARTING. A task already past PENDING (STARTING/RUNNING/RECOVERING)
matched no rows, raising `ManagedJobStatusError`, which the controller
escalated to FAILED_CONTROLLER and tore down the otherwise-healthy group.

Gate `set_starting` on `needs_launch(task_id)` so only fresh (None/PENDING)
tasks transition to STARTING, mirroring the single-task path's
`if not is_resume` guard. Add a regression test.

subject: [Server] Always exit on graceful shutdown even if request drain fails (#9986)
message:
[Server] Always exit on graceful shutdown even if request drain fails (#9986)

During graceful shutdown a worker sets block_requests=True early (to reject
new requests while in-flight ones drain) and then drains via a DB-backed
query for active requests. The drain runs in a daemon thread with no error
handling, so if the request backend is unreachable at that moment the query
raises (or the coordinator filelock blocks), the thread dies before
should_exit is set. The worker then stays up forever rejecting every request
with "server is shutting down", and never restarts to clear the block.

Wrap the drain in try/finally so should_exit and handle_exit always run,
bound the coordinator-lock wait with a timeout, and make the active-requests
query best-effort so a backend outage stops the drain instead of propagating.
A failed drain now still lets the process exit and be restarted.

Adds unit tests covering backend-unreachable, no-requests, and lock-timeout
paths.

subject: [API] Measure executor queue-wait per-enqueue, not since request creation (#9988)
message:
[API] Measure executor queue-wait per-enqueue, not since request creation (#9988)

* [API] Measure executor queue-wait per-enqueue, not since request creation

The sky_apiserver_queue_wait_seconds histogram observed
time.time() - request.created_at at dequeue, so a request that was
admitted promptly but later bounced back to the queue (retry/backoff,
broken process pool, or precondition wait) reported a wait that included
all the time spent outside the queue. This inflated the P95 and tripped
the executor-pool-full alert on healthy servers.

Move emission into the queue backend's get(), measuring time between the
entry's enqueue and its dequeue. Each put() (including re-enqueues)
stamps a fresh enqueue time, so paused/running time is naturally
excluded and the metric reflects true queue residency.

subject: [Jobs] Fix managed-job log GC on PostgreSQL and cover all terminal states (#9974)
message:
[Jobs] Fix managed-job log GC on PostgreSQL and cover all terminal states (#9974)

* [Jobs] Clean controller logs for all terminal jobs, not just those with downloaded task logs

* [Jobs] Fix managed-job log GC raising on PostgreSQL (schedule_state IS 'DONE')

The GC queries compared schedule_state with .is_(DONE.value), which renders
as `schedule_state IS 'DONE'`. PostgreSQL only allows IS with NULL/TRUE/FALSE,
so both queries raised a syntax error on every GC cycle and no logs were ever
cleaned on PG-backed deployments. SQLite accepts IS <string>, so unit tests
never caught it. Use == instead.

* [Jobs] Also clean controller logs of jobs cancelled while pending

A job cancelled while still PENDING (set_pending_cancelled) reaches DONE with
end_at never set. The controller-log query's having(max(end_at) IS NOT NULL)
filtered these out, so they were never marked cleaned and got re-scanned by the
group-by on every GC cycle. Since dropping the local_log_file gate let these
rows reach the group-by, treat a NULL max(end_at) as immediately cleanable
(they never ran, so there is no log to retain).

subject: [Debug Dump] Collect Kubernetes resources in debug dump (#9937)
message:
[Debug Dump] Collect Kubernetes resources in debug dump (#9937)

* [Core] Collect Kubernetes resources in debug dump

For a cluster running on Kubernetes, snapshot its related k8s objects
under clusters/<name>/kubernetes/ so an operator can inspect the cluster
like `kubectl get -o yaml` without needing kubectl access to it:

- the cluster's pods (one list-by-label call) and the events involving
  them (one namespace-wide pod-event query, filtered + grouped per pod)
- the resources SkyPilot creates, found by the skypilot-cluster-name
  label (Services, Deployments, PVCs, ConfigMaps, Secrets [values
  redacted], Ingresses)
- when the cluster uses Kueue (its pods carry the queue-name label): its
  Workload (by name), the namespace's LocalQueues, and the cluster-scoped
  ClusterQueues/ResourceFlavors/Topologies, trying CRD versions
  newest-first

apiVersion/kind are stamped back onto objects from list calls (Kubernetes
omits TypeMeta on list items) and verbose managedFields is stripped, so
the YAML matches `kubectl get -o yaml`. Every query is best-effort and
bounded by a request timeout: failures are recorded in errors.json and
never abort the dump.

Detection + coordinate extraction stay generic in sky/utils/debug_utils.py;
the queries + serialization live in a new sky/provision/kubernetes/debug.py.
Adds unit coverage for both.

* [Core] Split debug-dump k8s collection into per-cluster + per-context

Cluster-wide k8s info (GPU-metrics pods, the non-Workload Kueue objects:
ClusterQueues/LocalQueues/ResourceFlavors/Topologies) is shared across all
SkyPilot clusters on a kube context, so collecting it per cluster re-fetched
the identical objects once per cluster. Collect it once per unique context
under kubernetes_contexts/<sanitized-context>/, keep genuinely per-cluster
data (pods, events, labeled resources, the cluster's 1:1 Kueue Workload)
under clusters/<name>/kubernetes/, and link them via a context.json mapping.

Robustness for defunct contexts (tenants can have kube contexts that time
out): disable urllib3 retries on the debug clients so a failed call costs one
timeout (~5s) instead of ~4x, fast-fail both the per-context and per-cluster
paths on the first connection error, fetch unique contexts in parallel, and
always drop a context.json marker {context, reachable} so a reachable-but-bare
or unreachable context still appears in the dump.

The per-cluster path stays namespace-scoped (works under minimal RBAC); all
cluster-wide API calls live only in the per-context path and are best-effort.

subject: [Debug Dump] Collect Prometheus server container logs (#9993)
message:
[Debug Dump] Collect Prometheus server container logs (#9993)

* [Debug Dump] Collect Prometheus server container logs

The GPU-metrics debug dump captures the Prometheus server pod object, but the
pod's restart reason alone doesn't show why it died during startup -- the WAL
replay progress ("Replaying WAL...", per-segment loads) and any panic/abort
message live only in the container's own logs.

Collect the prometheus-server container's logs alongside the pod object: the
current container's tail and, when it has restarted, the previous (terminated)
container's logs -- the latter holds the boot-to-crash output of the instance
that actually failed. Tail-bounded and best-effort; a 400 on the previous read
(the container never restarted) is treated as "no previous", not an error.

* [Debug Dump] Dedupe identical previous log + record write errors

Two refinements to the prometheus-server container-log collection:

- Skip a previous-container log that is byte-for-byte identical to the current
  one. In a fast crash-loop the previous/current reads can resolve to the same
  container instance (mid-CrashLoopBackOff kubelet returns the last-terminated
  instance for both reads, and a restart can also fall between them), which
  otherwise writes a confusing duplicate file.
- Move the directory creation + file write inside the try block so a local
  OSError (full disk, permissions) is recorded best-effort instead of
  propagating and aborting the rest of the gpu_metrics collection.

Adds unit tests for both.
